symptom_text: Black Measles (also known as Esca) of grapevine produces striking interveinal chlorosis and necrosis on leaves, where the tissue between the veins turns yellow to reddish-brown while the veins themselves remain green, creating a distinctive 'tiger-stripe' pattern. On berries, small dark purple to black spots with lighter halos appear scattered across the fruit surface, giving the characteristic 'measles' appearance. Infected wood in cross-section reveals dark brown to black streaking and discoloration of the xylem tissue. Severely affected vines may exhibit sudden 'apoplexy,' wilting and collapsing rapidly during hot weather. Symptoms are distributed throughout the canopy and can affect leaves, berries, and woody tissues simultaneously.

pathogen.value: Fungal complex including Phaeoacremonium minimum, Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, and Fomitiporia mediterranea

affected_organs.value: Leaves, berries, woody canes and trunk
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Affected parts include leaves, fruit, and the woody parts of the vine including cordons, arms, and trunk.

visual_symptoms.value: Interveinal chlorosis and necrosis on leaves forming tiger-stripe pattern; dark spots with lighter halos on berries; dark streaking in wood
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Leaf symptoms appear as a 'tiger stripe' pattern with interveinal areas turning yellow to reddish brown while the veins remain green. Berries develop small, dark spots surrounded by a lighter halo, giving the fruit a measles-like appearance.

symptom_text: Grape black rot causes circular to irregularly shaped tan or brown lesions on leaves, typically 1/4 to 1/2 inch in diameter, with a dark brown to black border; tiny black pycnidia (fruiting bodies) are visible within the lesion centers. On young shoots, tendrils, and petioles, dark elongated cankers develop. Berries are the most severely affected organ: infected fruit initially shows a small white spot that rapidly enlarges, turning brown and then shriveling into hard, black, mummified berries (mummies) that remain attached to the cluster, often covered with black pycnidia arranged in a ring pattern.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Black rot of grape is caused by the ascomycetous fungus Guignardia bidwellii (Ellis) Viala & Ravaz.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Black rot can infect all green parts of the vine including leaves, shoots, petioles, tendrils, rachises, and berries.

visual_symptoms.value: Circular tan lesions with dark borders on leaves containing black pycnidia; dark cankers on shoots; berries turn brown then shrivel into black mummies covered with pycnidia
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Leaf lesions are circular, tan to brown, and have a dark brown to black border. Small, black pycnidia (fruiting bodies) form within the lesions. Infected berries first appear light brown, then turn dark brown to black, and eventually shrivel into hard, black mummies.

Grape downy mildew, caused by Plasmopara viticola, produces pale yellow to bright yellow-green oily or water-soaked lesions on the upper surface of leaves, often described as 'oil spots,' which are irregular to angular in shape and bounded by leaf veins. On the corresponding lower leaf surface, a dense white cottony or downy sporulation (sporangiophores and sporangia) develops under humid conditions. As lesions age, they turn brown and necrotic. Young shoots, tendrils, petioles, and developing berries can also be infected; infected berries turn grayish-white with sporulation before shriveling and turning brown, a condition known as 'gray rot' or 'hard rot' depending on the stage of infection.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Downy mildew of grape is caused by Plasmopara viticola, an oomycete pathogen that is not a true fungus.

affected_organs.value: Leaves, shoots, tendrils, petioles, flowers, and berries
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: All green parts of the vine are susceptible to infection, including leaves, shoots, tendrils, petioles, flowers, and berries.

visual_symptoms.value: Yellow oily spots on upper leaf surface; white downy sporulation on lower leaf surface; infected berries turn grayish and shrivel
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: On the upper surface of leaves, symptoms first appear as pale yellow, oily or water-soaked spots. Under humid conditions, a white downy growth (sporangiophores and sporangia) appears on the lower surface of leaves directly below the oily spots.

Gray mold of grape, caused by Botrytis cinerea, produces a characteristic gray to brown fuzzy sporulating mass (conidia) on infected tissues. On berries, infections begin as water-soaked, soft, brown lesions that rapidly expand to cover the entire berry surface, which then collapses and becomes covered with a dense gray powdery sporulation. Infected clusters show browning and rotting of individual berries that can spread to adjacent berries and rachis tissue. On shoots and leaves, irregular brown lesions with concentric zonation may appear, and infected flower clusters turn brown and shrivel. The disease is most severe under cool, wet, or humid conditions, and the gray dusty spore masses are the most diagnostic visual feature distinguishing this disease from other bunch rots.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Gray mold of grape is caused by the fungus Botrytis cinerea Pers.:Fr. (teleomorph: Botryotinia fuckeliana (de Bary) Whetzel).

affected_organs.value: Berries, clusters, rachis, shoots, leaves, flowers
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Botrytis can infect all green tissues of the grapevine including leaves, shoots, flowers, and fruit.

visual_symptoms.value: Gray to brown fuzzy sporulating masses on berries; water-soaked brown lesions expanding to cover berry surface; infected clusters show browning and collapse of berries covered with gray powdery spore masses
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Infected berries turn brown and soft, and under moist conditions, the characteristic gray sporulation of the fungus covers the surface of infected berries and clusters.

symptom_text: Grape leaf blight caused by Pseudocercospora vitis (Isariopsis leaf spot / leaf blight) produces irregular to angular, dark reddish-brown to black necrotic lesions on the upper leaf surface, often surrounded by a yellow chlorotic halo. Lesions typically begin as small spots that enlarge and coalesce, causing large blighted areas; affected tissue may dry out and fall away, leaving ragged holes. Dark olivaceous sporulation (conidiophores and conidia) may be visible on the lower leaf surface. Lesions are distributed across the blade, frequently near leaf margins and veins, and severe infections lead to premature defoliation.

pathogen.value: Pseudocercospora vitis (syn. Isariopsis clavispora; teleomorph: Mycosphaerella personata)

Grapevine leafroll disease causes distinctive downward rolling of leaf margins on mature leaves, typically appearing in late summer and early autumn. In red-fruited cultivars, affected leaves display striking interveinal reddening or purpling of the blade while the veins themselves remain green, creating a sharp color contrast across the leaf surface. In white-fruited cultivars, leaves turn yellow or chlorotic between the veins. Symptoms progress from the basal leaves upward along the shoot, and affected leaves often have a leathery texture. Clusters on infected vines may be smaller, with delayed and uneven berry ripening, reduced sugar accumulation, and poor color development in red varieties.

pathogen.value: Grapevine leafroll-associated viruses (GLRaVs), primarily GLRaV-1 and GLRaV-3

symptom_text: Grape powdery mildew presents as white to grayish-white, powdery or dusty fungal colonies that form on the surfaces of leaves, shoots, tendrils, and berry clusters. On leaves, the superficial mycelium appears as irregular, pale-yellow to white patches on the upper surface, often accompanied by a corresponding chlorotic or necrotic area on the lower surface. Infected young berries develop a characteristic webbing of white mycelium over their surface; as berries enlarge, the skin may crack or split, exposing seeds, and infected tissue turns brown to russet. Shoot tips and rachises may also be covered with the white powdery growth, and severely infected clusters can exhibit stunted, distorted berries with a rough, russeted texture distributed throughout the cluster.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Powdery mildew of grape is caused by the fungus Erysiphe necator Schwein. (synonym Uncinula necator (Schwein.) Burrill).

affected_organs.value: Leaves, shoots, tendrils, rachises, and berries

visual_symptoms.value: White to grayish-white powdery mycelial growth on leaves, shoots, and berries; infected berries may crack and turn brown; chlorotic patches on leaf surfaces
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Infected tissues are covered with a white to gray powdery growth of mycelium and conidia. Infected berries may crack open, exposing the seeds, and the skin and flesh turn brown.
